climate: Seasons this mild ripen Tempranillo, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc fully without cooking off their freshness.
Tempranillo sits in its sweet spot, so the wines can show the style it is known for.
Garnacha is at its cool limit. In cool years it can stay underripe, with green, sharp flavors.

soil.rock: Gravel drains fast and is poor, so roots go deep for water and food. It holds little water.
soil.top: The topsoil holds water well and drains at a steady pace, so vines rarely go thirsty or sit in wet ground. Its high pH can starve vines of iron and yellow the leaves, so growers plant lime-tolerant rootstocks.

land: The high ground runs about 5°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.
Gentle slopes. Enough tilt to drain cold air and rain away, which lowers frost risk, yet still easy to farm by machine.

sheet.place: Rioja is Spain's first DOCa, since 1991. It follows the upper Ebro for about 100 km, with Atlantic air in the west and Mediterranean warmth in the east. There are over 66,000 hectares of vines, on clay-limestone, ferrous clay and alluvial soils.
sheet.rules: Reds: Crianza is 2 years with 1 in oak. Reserva is 3 years with 1 in oak. Gran Reserva is 5 years with 2 in oak and 2 in bottle. Whites and rosados: 6 months in oak at least, then 2 years total for Reserva and 4 for Gran Reserva.

claims.claim: Rioja is a Denominación de Origen Calificada (DOCa), and was the first in Spain. The Consejo Regulador dates the qualified status to 1991 and says its wines have been protected since 1925.

The DOCa has four origin levels: DOCa Rioja, Vino de Zona, Vino de Pueblo and Vino de Viñedo Singular. Vino de Zona names Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa or Rioja Oriental. Vino de Pueblo covers any of the delimited municipalities.

Wikipedia says new classification rules came in 2018, focused on villages and vineyard sites. The Consejo page dates Viñedo Singular to 2017. Rioja Oriental is the newer name for what was called Rioja Baja.
The Consejo says Rioja has more than 66,000 hectares of vineyard in 144 municipalities: 118 in La Rioja, 18 in the Basque Country and 8 in Navarre.
Per-zone vineyard area, as second-hand Consejo figures: Rioja Alta about 27,900 ha, Rioja Oriental about 25,200 ha, Rioja Alavesa about 13,200 ha.

The region follows the upper Ebro valley, which runs west to east near its northern edge, over about 100 km from Haro in the west to Alfaro in the east. Seven tributary valleys cut into the south side.
The Sierra de Cantabria shelters the region from the north. The Demanda and Cameros ranges bound it to the south.

The climate mixes Atlantic and Mediterranean influences. The west leans Atlantic and the east is more Mediterranean, so Rioja Oriental is the warmest and driest zone. Average annual temperature is 12 to 14 C with about 2,000 sunshine hours.
Vineyards sit from about 300 m up to about 900 m on terraced hillside plots.
Zone altitudes: Rioja Alta about 400 to 600 m and Rioja Alavesa about 400 to 700 m.

Three main soil types: calcareous (clay-limestone) soils that are yellow-ochre, low in organic matter and rich in calcium; ferrous clay soils that are reddish-brown, deep and compact on the middle hills and higher ground; and alluvial soils that are sandy and stony on flat terraces by the Ebro and its tributaries.
Rioja Alta mixes clay-limestone, ferrous clay and alluvial soils. Rioja Alavesa is mostly clay-limestone. Rioja Oriental is mostly ferrous clay and alluvial.

Haro is at the western end of the region, in Rioja Alta. The Barrio de la Estación is a district of wineries beside the railway station. A rail line from Catalonia to Bilbao opened in 1864, and wineries were built beside the tracks from the 1870s.

Wineries in the Barrio de la Estación include CVNE (1879), Gómez Cruzado (1886), La Rioja Alta (1890), Bodegas Bilbaínas (1901), Muga (cellars moved there in 1970) and Roda (1987). López de Heredia is also in the district.
The usual explanation is that Rioja comes from Río Oja, a small tributary of the Tirón, which joins the Ebro just north of Haro. The name is first recorded in 1099. The origin is not settled.
Red grapes include Tempranillo, Garnacha, Mazuelo and Graciano. White grapes include Viura, Malvasía and Garnacha blanca. Tempranillo is about 88% of red plantings.
Red Crianza: 2 years total, at least 1 year in oak (225 litre barrels).
Red Reserva: 3 years total, at least 1 year in oak and at least 6 months in bottle.
Red Gran Reserva: 5 years total, at least 2 years in oak and 2 years in bottle.
White and rosado Crianza: at least 6 months in oak. The Consejo page gives no total time. Secondary sources say 18 months total.
White and rosado Reserva: 2 years total, with at least 6 months in oak.
White and rosado Gran Reserva: 4 years total, with at least 6 months in oak.
These are minimums. A wine can sit longer in barrel or bottle before release, which López de Heredia is known to do.
